nodes.label: Old Assyrian Assur
nodes.full: The merchant city-state of Assur before the kingdom — governed by its assembly and its eponym, living entirely off the caravan trade to Anatolia, and already deferring culturally to Babylon. See babylon-2004bc-1595bc.
nodes.src: background — see the folio babylon-2004bc-1595bc; Larsen, 'Ancient Kanesh' (2015).

nodes.label: The Neo-Assyrian Empire
nodes.full: The empire rebuilt from the Middle Assyrian core after the recovery began around 934 — the annalistic ideology, the holy-war theology, the deportation machine and the god Ashur all carried over. See assyria-911bc-609bc.
nodes.src: background — see the folio assyria-911bc-609bc.

nodes.label: Kassite Babylonia
nodes.full: The rival southern kingdom — from which Assyria takes its scholarship and literature, over which it fights a recurring frontier war, and which Tukulti-Ninurta and Tiglath-Pileser I each conquer. See babylon-1595bc-1155bc.
nodes.src: background — see the folio babylon-1595bc-1155bc.

nodes.label: The Aramaeans
nodes.full: The West-Semitic tribes of the Syrian steppe who cross the Euphrates in growing numbers from the twelfth century, cut Assyria off from the west, and nearly end the kingdom.
nodes.src: background — K. Lawson Younger, 'A Political History of the Arameans' (2016).

nodes.label: The Hittite Empire
nodes.full: The Anatolian great power that contests northern Syria with Assyria, watches its rise with alarm, is beaten by Tukulti-Ninurta at Nihriya, and collapses entirely around 1200.
nodes.src: background — Trevor Bryce, 'The Kingdom of the Hittites' (2005).

nodes.label: Ashur-uballit I founds the Assyrian state
nodes.full: As the kingdom of Mitanni was ground between the Hittites and Assyria, Ashur-uballit threw off its overlordship, took the title 'king of Assyria' rather than the old 'steward of the god Assur', wrote to Egypt as a fellow 'Great King', and married his granddaughter into the Kassite royal house — later marching into Babylon to avenge her son. He is the man who turned the merchant city-state of Assur into a kingdom.
nodes.src: A. K. Grayson, 'Assyrian Rulers of the Third and Second Millennia BC' (RIMA 1, 1987); the Amarna letters EA 15–16 (Moran 1992).

nodes.label: Adad-nirari I, the first conqueror
nodes.full: Adad-nirari I fought two wars against the rump Mitanni state of Hanigalbat, annexed it, and pushed Assyria's border to the Euphrates. He took the swaggering titles 'king of the totality' and 'king of all peoples', and his inscriptions swell from terse dedications into the boastful campaign narrative that becomes the Assyrian house style. He also beat the Kassites in a border battle at Sugagu.
nodes.src: RIMA 1 (Grayson 1987); the Adad-nirari–Hanigalbat wars in the royal annals and the Hittite correspondence.

nodes.label: Shalmaneser I crushes and colonises Mitanni
nodes.full: Shalmaneser I put down a Hittite-backed revolt of Hanigalbat, and — by his own count — blinded and deported fourteen thousand four hundred captives and scattered Assyrian forts and settlers across the whole dry-farming plain of the Jazira, turning the former Hurrian kingdom into an Assyrian province. He also campaigned in the Nairi highlands to the north and founded the city of Kalhu.
nodes.src: RIMA 1 (Grayson 1987); the Jazira settlement in Stefan Jakob, 'Mittelassyrische Verwaltung und Sozialstruktur' (2003).

nodes.label: Tukulti-Ninurta I — the peak
nodes.full: Tukulti-Ninurta I beat the Hittites, conquered Babylon and carried off both its king and its god, and campaigned deep into the Zagros and the Nairi lands. Then he built a huge new capital across the Tigris from Assur — Kar-Tukulti-Ninurta, 'Quay of Tukulti-Ninurta' — with a rival temple of Ashur 'in the new city', a move that set the old priesthood and nobility against him.
nodes.src: RIMA 1 (Grayson 1987); the new capital in the excavation reports of Walter Bachmann and later German work.

nodes.label: The murder of Tukulti-Ninurta
nodes.full: Besieged in his own new city by a faction of nobles, Tukulti-Ninurta was deposed and killed — Chronicle P names his son Ashur-nadin-apli as the leader. The new capital was abandoned almost at once; Assyria lost Babylon and its grip on the west; and the throne passed through a run of short reigns. The Assyrian empire's first bid ended in a palace coup.
nodes.src: 'Chronicle P'; the fall in Peter Machinist, 'The Epic of Tukulti-Ninurta I' (1978), and Grayson, RIMA 1.

nodes.label: The dark century
nodes.full: For most of a century Assyria was ruled by kings whose reigns are little more than names — Ashur-dan I the longest of them — under Babylonian, Elamite and steadily rising Aramaean pressure, with the western conquests lost. The records thin out. Assyria was a middling regional power holding its heartland and not much more.
nodes.src: RIMA 1 (Grayson 1987); the period's obscurity noted in Marc Van De Mieroop, 'A History of the Ancient Near East' (2016).

nodes.label: Ashur-resha-ishi I begins the recovery
nodes.full: Ashur-resha-ishi I beat off Aramaean raiders and repulsed a Babylonian invasion under Nebuchadnezzar I, rebuilt the temples of Assur, and restored the confidence of the Assyrian state. His reign is the platform from which his son launched the last and greatest Middle Assyrian revival.
nodes.src: A. K. Grayson, 'Assyrian Rulers of the Early First Millennium BC' (RIMA 2, 1991); the clash with Nebuchadnezzar I in the Babylonian sources.

nodes.label: Tiglath-Pileser I — the whirlwind
nodes.full: His clay prism claims forty-two campaigns in five years. He shattered twenty thousand Mushki — Phrygians — in the northern mountains, reached Lake Van and the Nairi lands, marched to the Mediterranean to cut cedar and take tribute from Byblos, Sidon and Arwad, sailed on the sea and speared a sea-creature, sacked Babylon, hunted elephants on the Habur and wild bulls in Lebanon, and stocked a library at Assur. It was the high-water mark of Middle Assyrian power.
nodes.src: A. K. Grayson, 'Assyrian Rulers of the Early First Millennium BC I' (RIMA 2, 1991), the Tiglath-Pileser I prisms.

nodes.label: Ashur-bel-kala and the rising tide
nodes.full: Ashur-bel-kala fought the Aramaeans in nearly every year of his reign — the 'Broken Obelisk' is his monument — campaigned as far as the coast, and made a marriage alliance with the Babylonian royal house. But the tribes kept crossing the Euphrates in greater numbers, and after him the effort to hold the west failed for good.
nodes.src: RIMA 2 (Grayson 1991); the 'Broken Obelisk' and the Ashur-bel-kala annals.

nodes.label: The reduction to the core
nodes.full: Within a generation Assyria held only the triangle of Assur, Nineveh, Arbela and Kalhu; the Aramaeans occupied the Jazira and the Habur and cut the roads west; and a poorly-recorded dark age set in that lasted until the recovery began around 934. But the state's machinery, the eponym list, the King List and the god Ashur all came through unbroken. The Neo-Assyrian Empire would be, consciously, this kingdom rebuilt.
nodes.src: J. A. Brinkman, 'Prelude to Empire' (1984); the continuity of institutions in Karen Radner, 'Ancient Assyria: A Very Short Introduction' (2015).

nodes.label: The fall of Mitanni and the deportation of Hanigalbat
nodes.full: Over two generations Assyria dismantled the Hurrian kingdom of Mitanni — annexing its rump, Hanigalbat, under Adad-nirari I, then crushing a Hittite-backed revolt under Shalmaneser I, who reports blinding and deporting fourteen thousand four hundred people. Assyrian forts and colonists took over the emptied plain. It is the first large-scale Assyrian conquest, and the first use of mass deportation as a tool of rule.
nodes.src: RIMA 1 (Grayson 1987); Stefan Jakob, 'Mittelassyrische Verwaltung und Sozialstruktur' (2003).

nodes.label: The battle of Nihriya against the Hittites
nodes.full: At Nihriya on the upper Tigris, Tukulti-Ninurta defeated the army of Tudhaliya IV, the last strong king of the Hittites, in a contest over the old Mitanni lands and the metal routes through the mountains. It is one of the very few times Assyria beat a Great Power in the field, and it hastened the decline of Hatti a generation before its final collapse.
nodes.src: Itamar Singer, 'The Battle of Nihriya and the End of the Hittite Empire' (ZA 1985); RIMA 1.

nodes.label: The conquest of Babylon
nodes.full: Tukulti-Ninurta broke the army of the Kassite king Kashtiliash IV, took him prisoner to Assur, sacked Babylon, pulled down its wall and carried the statue of Marduk north. For about seven years an Assyrian king ruled Babylonia. His court epic presents the whole campaign as the gods' judgement on a Kassite king who had broken his sworn oath. It is the first time Assyria held the south.
nodes.src: Peter Machinist, 'The Epic of Tukulti-Ninurta I' (1978); 'Chronicle P'; the Babylonian side in the folio babylon-1595bc-1155bc.

nodes.label: The forty-two campaigns of Tiglath-Pileser I
nodes.full: Tiglath-Pileser I's annals narrate a war machine at full stretch: the destruction of the Mushki in the north, campaigns into the Nairi lands and to Lake Van, the march to the sea to take Levantine tribute and cut cedar, and the sacking of Babylon. Fought almost every year, described campaign by campaign in the first person, it set the template — aggressive, annual, self-documented warfare — for the empire that came after.
nodes.src: RIMA 2 (Grayson 1991), the Tiglath-Pileser I annals.

nodes.label: The losing struggle with the Aramaeans
nodes.full: Tiglath-Pileser I records crossing the Euphrates twenty-eight times to chase the 'Ahlamu-Aramaeans'; Ashur-bel-kala fought them yearly. It made no lasting difference. The tribes kept coming, settled the Jazira and the Habur, founded their own small states, and cut Assyria off from the west. The Middle Assyrian kingdom was not conquered so much as slowly surrounded and starved.
nodes.src: K. Lawson Younger, 'A Political History of the Arameans' (2016); the annals in RIMA 2 (Grayson 1991).

nodes.label: The famine and the flight to the mountains
nodes.full: Assyrian texts of the decline record years of failed harvest so severe that people abandoned their towns for the hills and — the 'Broken Obelisk' says — ate their own children. Aramaean raiding and the loss of the Jazira grain supply compounded the crop failures. The military collapse and the subsistence collapse fed each other.
nodes.src: The famine passages in the Ashur-bel-kala texts (RIMA 2, Grayson 1991); discussed in Brinkman, 'Prelude to Empire' (1984).

nodes.label: The Middle Assyrian Laws
nodes.full: A set of law tablets copied under Tiglath-Pileser I from older material — the best preserved, Tablet A, deals with women — codifies a far harsher order than Hammurabi's Babylon. Veiling is regulated so that a slave or prostitute caught veiled is stripped and beaten; a husband may flog, pledge or mutilate his wife with little check; a woman who procures an abortion is impaled. It is the law of a militarised, patriarchal society.
nodes.src: Martha Roth, 'Law Collections from Mesopotamia and Asia Minor' (1997), pp. 153–194; G. R. Driver & J. C. Miles, 'The Assyrian Laws' (1935).

nodes.label: The palace decrees on the harem
nodes.full: A running series of royal edicts, from Ashur-uballit I to Tiglath-Pileser I, micromanaged the royal household — above all the women. They fix which quarters a palace woman may enter, who may look at or speak to her, the exact deference owed her, and the mutilations that await a courtier or eunuch who breaks the rules or lets a woman out of place. The control of women is written into the constitution of the court.
nodes.src: Roth, 'Law Collections' (1997), pp. 195–209; the 'Harem Edicts' first edited by Ernst Weidner.

nodes.label: The dunnu and the provincial grid
nodes.full: Assyria held the conquered Jazira through a network of fortified farm-estates — the dunnu — and provincial governors, tied to the centre by roads, the corvée and a paper trail. The dunnu of Tell Sabi Abyad, run by the steward Tammitte for an absent royal-family lord, has left an archive that documents one such estate almost day by day: its ploughing, its herds, its deportee labour, its grain sent to the capital, its defence against raiders.
nodes.src: Frans Wiggermann, 'Agriculture in the Northern Balikh Valley: The Case of Middle Assyrian Tell Sabi Abyad' (2000); Bleda Düring, 'The Imperialisation of Assyria' (2020).

nodes.label: The eponym and the Assyrian King List
nodes.full: Assyria dated its years not by the king's reign but by the limmu, an official — the king first, then the great officers in rotation — who gave his name to the year. And it kept the Assyrian King List, naming every ruler, his father and his years back to legendary 'kings who lived in tents'. Together with the Babylonian lists and the Venus Tablet, the King List is the framework on which every Mesopotamian date hangs — and it is also a claim of unbroken legitimate succession.
nodes.src: The Assyrian King List (I. J. Gelb, JNES 1954); the eponym system in Alan Millard, 'The Eponyms of the Assyrian Empire' (1994).

nodes.label: The king as the steward of Ashur
nodes.full: The Assyrian king was the išši'akku — the steward or vicar — of the god Ashur, who was himself the deified city and state. The king waged war, built temples and gave judgement not in his own name but on the god's behalf, and reported back to him. Unlike the god-kings of Ur, the Assyrian ruler was never divine; he was a priest and a general in the service of a god who was Assyria itself.
nodes.src: Beate Pongratz-Leisten, 'Religion and Ideology in Assyria' (2015); Peter Machinist, 'Kingship and Divinity in Imperial Assyria'.

nodes.label: The grant, the corvée and the god's offering
nodes.full: Middle Assyrian kings granted estates and their people to officials and temples, recorded on clay — the Assyrian counterpart of the Kassite boundary stone. Subjects owed the ilku, a mix of labour corvée and military service. And a levy on the provinces, the ginā'u, funded the daily offerings to Ashur, tracked so carefully that a whole administrative archive from Assur is given over to accounting the god's meals.
nodes.src: J. N. Postgate, 'The Land of Assur and the Yoke of Assur' (1992); the ginā'u archive studied by Jaume Llop and Betina Faist.

nodes.label: The god who is the state
nodes.full: Ashur is unlike any other Mesopotamian god: no myth, no consort by origin, no place in the cosmic story — he began simply as the holiness of the rock and the city of Assur, and grew into the personification of the whole Assyrian nation and its drive to expand. To be Assyrian was to serve Ashur; his temple on the cliff above the Tigris was the physical and ideological centre of the kingdom.
nodes.src: Beate Pongratz-Leisten, 'Religion and Ideology in Assyria' (2015); the Ashur temple in Walter Andrae's excavation reports.

nodes.label: The campaign as holy war
nodes.full: The Assyrian king marched 'at the command of Ashur', with the god's emblem carried at the head of the army; he dedicated the prisoners and the plunder to Ashur; and on his return he delivered a formal written 'letter to the god', an account of the campaign read aloud in the temple. It is the earliest fully worked-out theology of a nation's wars as acts of worship — a template the Neo-Assyrian empire would run at industrial scale.
nodes.src: Pongratz-Leisten (2015); the 'letter to the god' genre traced from Tukulti-Ninurta forward in Grayson, RIMA 1–2.

nodes.label: Ishtar of Nineveh and of Arbela
nodes.full: The war-goddess Ishtar had two great houses in the Assyrian heartland, at Nineveh and at Arbela, and she was the king's personal patron and his companion in battle — the fierce, unpredictable female deity at the centre of Assyrian devotion. The temple of Ishtar at Nineveh was among the oldest and wealthiest in Assyria, rebuilt by king after king.
nodes.src: Barbara Nevling Porter's studies of Assyrian Ishtar; the Nineveh Ishtar temple in Julian Reade's work.

nodes.label: The first Assyrian library
nodes.full: Tiglath-Pileser I assembled at Assur a working collection of tablets — omen series, hymns, epics, lexical lists, an early corpus of celestial omens — some of it copied locally, some carried back as loot from Babylon. This 'Middle Assyrian library' is the seed of the great royal libraries of Nineveh five centuries later, and the point at which Assyria became a keeper of the cuneiform tradition rather than only a borrower of it.
nodes.src: Olof Pedersén, 'Archives and Libraries in the City of Assur' (1985–86); Ernst Weidner on the library of Tiglath-Pileser I.

nodes.label: No decision without the omen
nodes.full: No campaign was launched, no governor appointed and no temple begun without extispicy. The corps of diviners put the question to the sun-god Shamash and the storm-god Adad, sacrificed a lamb, and read the answer in the markings of its liver and lungs. The omen was the channel through which the will of Ashur reached the king; a bad reading could stop an army on the march.
nodes.src: Ulla Koch, 'Secrets of Extispicy' (2005); the Assyrian practice in Ivan Starr, 'Queries to the Sungod' (SAA 4, 1990), reading back from the Neo-Assyrian corpus.

nodes.label: The royal tombs and the line of Assur
nodes.full: The Middle Assyrian kings were buried in vaulted stone chambers under the Old Palace at Assur, and the kispum meal fed the royal dead each month. The unbroken descent of the 'sons of Assur' — traced in the King List all the way back to legendary rulers 'who lived in tents' — was itself an article of the Assyrian faith: the nation, its god and its royal line were one continuous thing.
nodes.src: Walter Andrae's excavation of the Assur tombs; Olof Pedersén (1985–86); the ideology in Pongratz-Leisten (2015).

nodes.label: The painted palace
nodes.full: The Middle Assyrian palaces had their plastered walls painted — geometric borders of guilloche and rosette, and figural friezes of processions and palmettes, in red, black, blue and white. Fragments survive from Kar-Tukulti-Ninurta and Assur. It is the first Assyrian monumental interior decoration, and the direct ancestor of the carved stone wall-reliefs that line the palaces of the Neo-Assyrian kings.
nodes.src: Walter Andrae on the Assur and Kar-Tukulti-Ninurta wall paintings; Julian Reade, 'Assyrian Sculpture' (1983), on the antecedents of the reliefs.

nodes.label: The cult-pedestal of Tukulti-Ninurta
nodes.full: A carved stone pedestal from Assur shows King Tukulti-Ninurta twice over — once striding forward, once kneeling — before a standing emblem of the stylus of the scribal god on a matching pedestal. Showing the king in motion, and in the act of personal worship, is rare in Assyrian art, which usually freezes the ruler in static majesty. It is a small, unusual masterpiece.
nodes.src: Vorderasiatisches Museum, Berlin (VA 8146); Julian Reade, 'Assyrian Sculpture' (1983).

nodes.label: The Middle Assyrian seal
nodes.full: Middle Assyrian seal-cutters worked in a vigorous, naturalistic manner — real landscapes with trees and rolling ground, animals caught in violent motion, a winged demon dragging down a stag, hunters and their prey rendered with anatomical care. It is widely held to be some of the finest cylinder-seal engraving of the entire ancient Near East, a brief high point between the Kassite style and the Neo-Assyrian.
nodes.src: Anton Moortgat, 'Vorderasiatische Rollsiegel' (1940); Dominique Collon, 'First Impressions: Cylinder Seals in the Ancient Near East' (1987).

nodes.label: The invention of the royal annal
nodes.full: The Assyrian kings turned the building-dedication inscription into something new: a year-by-year, first-person account of the king's campaigns — 'in my accession year I marched against the land of X; in my first regnal year against Y' — structured by the regnal year, added to each season, and meant to last. It becomes the signature Assyrian literary form and the single most important narrative source for five centuries of Near Eastern history.
nodes.src: A. K. Grayson, 'Assyrian and Babylonian Chronicles' and 'Histories and Historians of the Ancient Near East' (1980); Mario Liverani on the annalistic genre.

nodes.label: The Tukulti-Ninurta Epic
nodes.full: A long Akkadian poem, the first Assyrian literary epic, tells how the Kassite king Kashtiliash broke a sworn treaty, how Marduk and the gods of Babylon therefore abandoned their city, and how Ashur's champion Tukulti-Ninurta was righteously sent to punish it. Part battle narrative, part legal indictment, part theology, it is a sophisticated piece of state poetry — the conquest of Babylon set to verse as an act of divine justice.
nodes.src: Peter Machinist, 'The Epic of Tukulti-Ninurta I: A Study in Middle Assyrian Literature' (PhD, 1978); Benjamin Foster, 'Before the Muses' (2005).

nodes.label: Assyria takes the Babylonian canon
nodes.full: Middle Assyrian scholars copied and studied the standard Babylonian series — the omen compendia, the medical and incantation handbooks, the lexical lists, the epics — importing the whole apparatus of cuneiform learning wholesale. Assyrian scholarship at this stage is frankly derivative; but the copying is part of how the tradition came through the Bronze Age collapse, and Assur becomes a second home for it alongside Babylon.
nodes.src: Olof Pedersén, 'Archives and Libraries in the City of Assur' (1985–86); the Middle Assyrian scholarly tablets from Assur.

nodes.label: The annal as a way of thinking about the past
nodes.full: The Assyrian royal annal is more than a literary form — it is a distinctive practice of recording: strictly ordered by the regnal year and the campaign, written in the first person, cumulative, added to each season, and understood as an official account rendered to the god of everything the king has done. It fixes a template for how a state remembers and reports itself that lasts to the end of Assyria.
nodes.src: A. K. Grayson, 'Histories and Historians of the Ancient Near East: Assyria and Babylonia' (Orientalia 1980).

nodes.label: The King List as chronological reasoning
nodes.full: The Assyrian King List is a genuine instrument of chronology: a continuous sequence of kings, each with his father and his years, cross-checkable against the separate eponym sequence and against dated contacts with Babylon and Egypt. It is a piece of applied historical reasoning — and the modern dating of the entire ancient Near East, Egypt included, is still anchored to it.
nodes.src: I. J. Gelb, 'Two Assyrian King Lists' (JNES 1954); Shigeo Yamada, 'The Editorial History of the Assyrian King List' (ZA 1994).

nodes.label: Watching the sky for the king
nodes.full: The Middle Assyrian court took up the practice — central to the later empire — of having scholars watch the heavens and report the ominous phenomena to the king with an interpretation and, where possible, a ritual to avert the evil. The early tablets of the celestial-omen series Enuma Anu Enlil are among the Assur scholarly finds. Astrology was becoming an instrument of Assyrian statecraft.
nodes.src: Francesca Rochberg, 'The Heavenly Writing' (2004); the Assur Enuma Anu Enlil manuscripts (Pedersén 1985–86).

nodes.label: The provincial north and the classical south
nodes.full: Assyrians spoke a distinct dialect of Akkadian and wrote in a distinct hand, and they knew it. Yet they took their gods' myths, their scholarship, their literature and their measure of high culture wholesale from Babylon, which they regarded as ancient and authoritative even as they conquered it. This self-conscious relationship — the militarised, 'provincial' north deferring culturally to the 'classical' south it dominated — runs through the whole of Assyrian history.
nodes.src: Peter Machinist, 'The Assyrians and their Babylonian Problem' (1984); Grant Frame on Assyrian–Babylonian cultural relations.

nodes.label: The dunnu and the exploitation of the Jazira
nodes.full: The productive backbone of the Middle Assyrian empire was the fortified estate. Each dunnu grew grain, oil and wool on the conquered plain, sent a share to the capital and the army, and was run by a resident steward for a lord who lived at court. The Tell Sabi Abyad archive shows one such operation in close-up — its ploughing schedule, its herds, its deportee workforce, its granary, its wagons rolling east.
nodes.src: Frans Wiggermann, 'Agriculture in the Northern Balikh Valley' (2000); J. N. Postgate, 'Bronze Age Bureaucracy' (2014).

nodes.label: Deportation as economic policy
nodes.full: When Assyria conquered a land it moved its people. Shalmaneser I claims to have deported fourteen thousand four hundred from Hanigalbat; the practice recurs. Uprooting the defeated broke their capacity to resist, and setting them to farm Assyrian estates put productive labour where the state wanted it. The Middle Assyrian kings invented the tool; the Neo-Assyrian empire would run it on an industrial scale.
nodes.src: A. K. Grayson, RIMA 1 (1987); the practice traced forward in Bustenay Oded, 'Mass Deportations and Deportees in the Neo-Assyrian Empire' (1979).

nodes.label: Feeding the god Ashur
nodes.full: A levy on every province, the ginā'u, funded the daily offerings set before Ashur in his temple — bread, beer, meat, fruit, oil — and a whole administrative archive from Assur is devoted to accounting the god's meals province by province. Provisioning the deified state was itself a central fiscal operation: to pay the ginā'u was to acknowledge that one belonged to Assyria.
nodes.src: The ginā'u archive from Assur, studied by Jaume Llop and Betina Faist; Postgate, 'The Land of Assur' (1992).

nodes.label: Overland trade after Kanesh
nodes.full: With the Old Assyrian Anatolian trade centuries gone, Assyrian commerce was overland caravan traffic in metals — copper, tin, and iron beginning to appear — in textiles and in slaves, moving along the Tigris and toward Babylonia and Syria, much of it on royal or temple account. As the Aramaeans took the western roads, this trade became first dangerous and then largely impossible.
nodes.src: Betina Faist, 'Der Fernhandel des assyrischen Reiches zwischen dem 14. und 11. Jahrhundert v. Chr.' (2001).

nodes.label: A political economy built for war
nodes.full: The Middle Assyrian state was organised around the yearly campaign: the dunnu grain fed the army, plunder and tribute fed the treasury, the ilku obligation supplied the labour and the soldiers. It worked while Assyria was winning and expanding. When the Jazira and the trade routes were lost to the Aramaeans, the machine had nothing left to consume, and the kingdom starved.
nodes.src: J. N. Postgate, 'Bronze Age Bureaucracy' (2014); F. M. Fales, 'Guerra e pace in Assiria' (2010).

nodes.label: The frontier fort as a kit
nodes.full: The Middle Assyrian dunnu and provincial fort was a standardised design — a mud-brick tower inside a walled enclosure, with storerooms, a well and a small shrine — that could be dropped along a road or a river to hold new ground. Replicable, defensible and self-supplying, it was the physical technology of Assyrian expansion, and the model the empire would build on for centuries.
nodes.src: Bleda Düring, 'The Imperialisation of Assyria: An Archaeological Approach' (2020); the Sabi Abyad dunnu (Akkermans).

nodes.label: Iron enters use
nodes.full: Iron tools and weapons turn up in growing numbers in Middle Assyrian contexts — still rare, still costly, but no longer curiosities. The Assyrian north, close to the ore of Anatolia and the Zagros and to smiths who knew how to work it, is exactly where the shift from bronze to iron would first take hold. The folio sits right on the metal-age threshold.
nodes.src: Jane Waldbaum, 'From Bronze to Iron' (1978); Anthony Snodgrass, 'The Coming of the Age of Iron' (1980).

nodes.label: The Assyrian military machine takes form
nodes.full: The Middle Assyrian army combined the light chariot with a growing body of disciplined heavy infantry — the powerful composite bow, the long thrusting spear, scale armour — and the first crude siege methods, the ram and the earthen assault ramp. It was already an unusually organised and aggressive force. The Neo-Assyrians would refine every part of it into the most effective army of the ancient world.
nodes.src: F. M. Fales, 'Guerra e pace in Assiria' (2010); the equipment reconstructed from the annals and from later reliefs.

nodes.label: The building of Kar-Tukulti-Ninurta
nodes.full: Tukulti-Ninurta's new capital across the Tigris from Assur was a full-scale royal foundation: a diverted canal to water it, a great raised terrace carrying a palace and a temple of Ashur, painted plaster and glazed decoration, a planned street grid. It was one of the largest building projects of the age — and it was abandoned within a generation of the king's murder.
nodes.src: Tilman Eickhoff, 'Kār Tukulti Ninurta: Eine mittelassyrische Kult- und Residenzstadt' (1985); recent German re-excavation.

nodes.label: Assyria's brief seat at the top table
nodes.full: Ashur-uballit I wrote to the Egyptian court with gifts and the greeting of one Great King to another — and won a place, briefly, in the small circle of powers that dealt as equals. It infuriated the Kassite king, who insisted the Assyrians were his vassals. The moment did not last: for the rest of the Middle Assyrian period Assyria's foreign policy was, overwhelmingly, war.
nodes.src: The Amarna letters EA 15–16 (Moran 1992); Burna-Buriash's protest is EA 9.

nodes.label: The struggle with Babylonia begins
nodes.full: From Ashur-uballit's intervention onward, Assyria and Babylonia were locked in the relationship that defines the rest of Assyrian history: a recurring war over the middle-Tigris border, the occasional Assyrian conquest of the south, a deep cultural debt running north — Assyria took its gods' myths, its scholarship and its literature from Babylon — and dynastic marriages between the two courts. Rival, teacher and prize, all at once.
nodes.src: The 'Synchronistic History'; J. A. Brinkman, 'Materials and Studies for Kassite History' I (1976).

nodes.label: The Hittite frontier and the fall of Hatti
nodes.full: Assyria and the Hittites contested the old Mitanni lands of northern Syria, and the Hittite kings watched Assyria's rise with open alarm in their treaty texts. Tukulti-Ninurta beat them at Nihriya. Then, around 1200, the Hittite empire collapsed entirely — and Assyria, having outlasted it, reached briefly toward the vacuum in the north-west before the Aramaeans closed it off.
nodes.src: Itamar Singer, 'The Battle of Nihriya and the End of the Hittite Empire' (1985); Trevor Bryce, 'The Kingdom of the Hittites' (2005).

nodes.label: Tiglath-Pileser I reaches the Mediterranean
nodes.full: Tiglath-Pileser I marched to the 'Upper Sea', cut cedar in the Lebanon for the temples of Assur, took tribute from Byblos, Sidon and Arwad, boarded a ship and killed a sea-creature he calls a nahiru, and received from the king of Egypt a crocodile and a large monkey as curiosities. It is the first time an Assyrian army touched the Levantine coast — a small foretaste of the empire that would rule it three centuries on.
nodes.src: A. K. Grayson, RIMA 2 (1991), the Tiglath-Pileser I annals.

nodes.label: The Aramaeans cross the Euphrates
nodes.full: From the mid-twelfth century West-Semitic Aramaean tribes crossed the Euphrates in mounting numbers — raiding, then settling, then founding their own small states, Bit-Adini, Bit-Bahiani, Bit-Zamani, across the Jazira and the Habur. They cut Assyria off from the west, occupied its lost province, and permanently changed the population and the language of the whole northern Fertile Crescent. Aramaic would in time replace Akkadian across the Near East.
nodes.src: K. Lawson Younger, 'A Political History of the Arameans' (2016); Edward Lipiński, 'The Aramaeans: Their Ancient History, Culture, Religion' (2000).

nodes.label: The rain-fed Assyrian triangle
nodes.full: The Assyrian heartland is a compact triangle on the upper Tigris — Assur on its cliff, Nineveh, Arbela, and later Kalhu — where just enough rain falls to grow grain without irrigation, backed by the Zagros foothills and the Jebel Sinjar. It is small, defensible, and self-feeding: the opposite of the vast, canal-dependent, slowly salting alluvium of the Babylonian south. This is the northern pole of the north–south divide the folio pair traces.
nodes.src: The Assyrian core in Karen Radner, 'Ancient Assyria: A Very Short Introduction' (2015); the geography contrasted in Marc Van De Mieroop, 'A History of the Ancient Near East' (2016).

nodes.label: The Jazira — the contested middle
nodes.full: Between Assyria and Syria lie the dry-farming plains of the Khabur and Balikh — the Jazira. Assyria conquered it from Mitanni, colonised it with the dunnu grid, and then lost it to the Aramaeans. It was fought over for the next fifteen hundred years — by Assyria and Babylon, then the Aramaeans, then the Achaemenids, the Romans and Sasanians, the Byzantines and the Arabs. The middle ground of Mesopotamia has always been where its wars are decided.
nodes.src: Bleda Düring, 'The Imperialisation of Assyria' (2020); the long-term contest in the Jazira's settlement history.

nodes.label: The Bronze Age crisis and a bare survival
nodes.full: Assyria came through the systemic crisis of around 1200 better than the powers of the Mediterranean rim — it had, after all, just beaten the Hittites. But the Aramaean flood and the collapse of the international trade system that followed reduced the kingdom, over the next century and a half, to its bare core. It survived where Hatti and Mycenae did not — but only just, and only its heartland.
nodes.src: Eric Cline, '1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed' (2014); the Assyrian trajectory in Grayson, RIMA 2 (1991).

nodes.label: The dark age that kept the memory of empire
nodes.full: The century and a half after 1050 is thinly recorded, and Assyria held only Assur, Nineveh, Arbela and Kalhu. But everything essential came through the dark age intact: the state machinery, the eponym list, the King List, the annalistic way of recording, the theology of the god's war, the deportation system, and Ashur himself. When the recovery began under Ashur-dan II around 934, the Neo-Assyrian Empire was consciously this kingdom rebuilt.
nodes.src: J. A. Brinkman, 'Prelude to Empire' (1984); the continuity argument in Karen Radner (2015).

nodes.label: The veiled woman of the Assyrian Laws
nodes.full: The Middle Assyrian law polices the veil obsessively: a wife, a married concubine and a palace woman must veil in public; a slave woman and a prostitute must not, on pain of a beating and having their clothes taken. Any citizen who sees a woman wrongly veiled may seize her and bring her to the palace gate to be denounced. A woman's status was made visible on her body and enforced by every passing man — a policing of women with no parallel in the Babylonian record.
nodes.src: Middle Assyrian Laws, Tablet A §40 (Roth, 'Law Collections', 1997); discussed in Julia Assante and in Sarah Shectman on veiling.

nodes.label: The deportee on the Balikh
nodes.full: A man marched from the Khabur or the Nairi highlands to an estate on the Balikh was counted in the dunnu's ledgers alongside its oxen and its grain — cut off from home, set to plough land that was not his for a lord he would never meet, sometimes blinded so that he could not run. Deportation was Assyria's method of turning a conquest into a workforce, and this was the life it produced.
nodes.src: The Tell Sabi Abyad archive (Wiggermann 2000); the treatment of deportees in Bustenay Oded (1979).

nodes.label: The steward of a fortress estate
nodes.full: Tammitte ran the dunnu of Sabi Abyad for an absent royal-family lord: he kept the crop accounts and the labour rosters, sent the harvest upriver, corresponded with the palace, judged small disputes, and organised the estate's defence against the raiders who came out of the steppe. He is imperial middle management on the frontier — the person on whom the whole colonial system actually rested.
nodes.src: Frans Wiggermann, 'Agriculture in the Northern Balikh Valley' (2000); the Sabi Abyad letters (Wiggermann; Akkermans).

nodes.label: The soldier of the yearly campaign
nodes.full: An Assyrian man owed the ilku — labour and military service — and in most years that meant marching. He was mustered in the spring, sent to the mountains or the desert edge, fed on the grain of the frontier estates and on what the army could seize, and rewarded, if the campaign went well, with a share of the plunder and of the captives. He was the human component of a state organised, as a matter of routine, for war.
nodes.src: J. N. Postgate, 'Bronze Age Bureaucracy' (2014); F. M. Fales, 'Guerra e pace in Assiria' (2010).

nodes.label: The scholar-priest of Assur
nodes.full: The Assyrian man of learning was several things at once: the bārû who took the omens before the army moved and could halt it with a bad reading; the ummânu who copied the Babylonian series in the palace library; the priest who prepared Ashur's daily meal and read the king his god's commands. Junior in prestige to the scholars of Babylon, this class was nonetheless the keeper of the whole tradition in the north.
nodes.src: Olof Pedersén, 'Archives and Libraries in the City of Assur' (1985–86); Beate Pongratz-Leisten, 'Religion and Ideology in Assyria' (2015).
